passage: At the badminton club's front desk, Arnab slid a laminated card across to Gopika. Weekday mornings: ₹1,500 a month. All-day access: ₹2,800. All-day with a locker: ₹2,850. "Most people take the last one," he said. Gopika smiled, laid her palm flat over the middle line and looked only at the other two. Then she took out the notebook she had brought and read her own list aloud: "Budget, two thousand. Play before work, three days a week. No locker needed, I live five minutes away." She looked up. "Weekday mornings, please." Arnab raised his eyebrows. "Most people don't say no to the locker." "Most people didn't write a list first," she said, and signed.

qa.q: What did Gopika lay her palm over?
qa.a: The middle line on the card, the all-day access plan.

qa.q: Why do you think Gopika brought a written list to the club?
qa.a: She seemed to expect the offer's layout might push her, so she wanted her own budget and needs written down beforehand to decide by them.

qa.q: Which steps made Gopika's choice sound?
qa.a: Covering the option nobody would pick, then reading her own list, a budget, morning play and no need for a locker, and choosing the plan that matched it.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel when Gopika picks the cheapest plan?
qa.a: Arnab seems surprised, since most people take the locker plan, and may notice for the first time how much the card's layout usually does the choosing.

grounding: A young woman covers the option nobody would pick and chooses a club plan by her own written budget and needs, not the layout of the offer.

passage:
Hi Mahima,
You asked how I finally chose a laptop. The secret is a pencil. The website showed three: one with 8 GB memory for ₹42,000, one with 16 GB for ₹61,000, and one with 16 GB plus a bigger screen for ₹62,000. Everything on the page was designed to make me want the last one. So I printed the page and struck through the ₹61,000 one, because nobody would ever choose it. Then I wrote my own list: budget ₹50,000, spreadsheets and video calls, light enough for the train. Against that list, the ₹42,000 one wins easily. The big-screen one would have been lovely and wrong. Try the pencil when you pick your phone.
Deepak

qa.q: What was Deepak's budget?
What did Deepak think the website was trying to do?
qa.a: Deepak felt wary, sensing the page was built to push the ₹62,000 laptop by using the ₹61,000 one to make it look like a bargain.

qa.q: Why was striking through the middle option useful before writing the list?
qa.a: Once the option nobody would choose was gone, the bigger laptop stopped looking like a deal, so Deepak could compare the rest against Deepak's own budget and needs.

qa.q: How might Mahima use this email when choosing a phone?
qa.a: Mahima could list the options, cross out any that seem to be there only to push another, and write down Mahima's own needs first.

grounding: A young adult strikes out the decoy option and chooses a laptop by a written list of their own budget and needs.

passage: Wasim, the caterer tried the oldest trick on me. I'm Suraj, the brother in charge of food for my sister's engagement, and I had three packages: Simple at ₹350 a plate, Deluxe at ₹620, and Royal at ₹640 with two extra sweets and a live counter. The owner kept tapping Royal. "Twenty rupees more, sir, and so much more!" I asked for a minute, took a photo of the menu card, went out to the car and covered Deluxe with my thumb on the screen. Then I opened the note I'd made with Amma the night before: 150 guests, vegetarian, ₹60,000 in total, and Dadi can't eat very spicy food. Simple, with one added sweet, fit every line. Royal didn't. I walked back in and ordered it. The owner looked disappointed. Amma was thrilled.

qa.q: How many guests were on Suraj's note?
Why do you think Suraj stepped out to the car before deciding?
qa.a: Suraj seemed to feel pressured by the owner's tapping and the menu layout, and wanted a quiet minute to decide by the family's list instead.

qa.q: Which steps turned the decision around?
qa.a: Covering Deluxe to remove the odd option, then checking the packages against the note made with Amma: guest count, vegetarian food, the total budget and Dadi's needs.

qa.q: How might Amma feel about the way Suraj ordered?
qa.a: Amma helped make the list, so she is likely thrilled that the food fits the budget and the family's needs rather than the caterer's push. 😊

grounding: A young man removes the decoy catering package and decides by a written list of guests, budget and needs rather than the layout of the offer.

passage: I'm Zainab, Rehana's cousin, and I went with her to the wedding photographer's studio in Hyderabad last month. The man laid out a glossy brochure. Silver: ₹40,000, one photographer, soft copies. Gold: ₹75,000, two photographers, no album, no drone. Platinum: ₹78,000, two photographers, album, drone shots. 'Everyone takes Platinum, madam,' he said. I was already nodding. Rehana just folded the brochure so Gold was hidden underneath. Then she took a folded paper out of her handbag. I peeked: 'Budget 50,000. Must: good family photos, soft copies. Don't need: drone.' She read it twice, then looked only at Silver and Platinum. 'Silver, please. We'll print an album ourselves.' The man tried twice more to show Gold. Rehana didn't unfold it. Outside, she laughed and said, 'That middle one was only there for me to look at.' I still don't know how she stayed so calm.

qa.q: What did Rehana's written list say about her budget?
What was Zainab feeling during the photographer's pitch, compared with Rehana?
qa.a: Zainab was already nodding along to Platinum, while Rehana stayed calm, which left Zainab impressed and a little puzzled.

qa.q: Which steps did Rehana take to avoid being steered, and why did they work?
qa.a: She folded the brochure to hide Gold, then compared the rest only against her written list of budget and needs, so the layout couldn't push her.

qa.q: How might the photographer have felt when Rehana wouldn't unfold the brochure?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated, since the Gold package was there to make Platinum look like the obvious choice and it didn't work on her.

grounding: A cousin watches a young woman hide the package nobody would pick and choose a photographer by her own written budget and needs.

passage:
Monday: Farhan, twenty-four and preparing for the state services exam, opened a coaching site. Recorded lectures: ₹6,000. Live classes, no mock tests: ₹11,500. Live classes with mock tests and doubt sessions: ₹12,000. 'Five hundred more for everything!' Naveen said over his shoulder. Farhan almost paid. Instead he closed the laptop.
Wednesday: at his desk he printed the page and stuck a sticky note over the middle plan. Nobody would ever pick it. Then he wrote his own list: 'Budget: 8,000. Weak area: answer writing. Need: mock tests. Don't need: live lectures, I study better alone at night.'
Saturday: he found the recorded plan could add mock tests separately for ₹1,500. Total ₹7,500. He paid it. Naveen shook his head. 'You're losing the live classes.' 'I'd have skipped them,' Farhan said, tapping his list. 'I decided with this, not with their page.'

qa.q: How much did Farhan pay in the end?
qa.a: He paid ₹7,500 for the recorded plan plus mock tests.

qa.q: Why did Farhan close the laptop on Monday instead of paying?
qa.a: He felt the pull of 'five hundred more for everything' but seemed unsure it was right for him, so he wanted time to think before deciding.

qa.q: Which steps helped Farhan decide, and why did they work?
qa.a: He covered the middle plan with a sticky note and wrote his own list of budget, weak area and needs, so he chose by his needs, not the page layout.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Farhan's final choice?
qa.a: Naveen thinks Farhan is missing out on live classes, because he is still judging by the page's offer rather than by Farhan's study habits.

grounding: Over several days a young man covers the option nobody would pick and chooses a coaching plan from a written list of his budget and needs.
